title: Many values, held together
idea: MEET the idea of a collection: sometimes a problem is about a whole group of values at once, not a single number. Thinking, almost no code.

exercises.prompt: So far, a variable has held ONE value at a time. But some problems are about MANY values. Which of these is about many values at once?
options: The test scores of everyone in a class
exercises.explanation: One class has many scores. When a problem talks about a whole group like that, a single variable isn't enough — we need something that holds many values.

exercises.prompt: Which everyday thing is most like 'many values held together in order'?
exercises.explanation: A shopping list is many items, written in order, as one thing. That is exactly the idea of a collection.

exercises.prompt: A single variable like score = 7 is a good fit when a problem is about one value.
exercises.explanation: One value, one variable — perfect. It's when there are MANY values that we reach for a collection instead.

exercises.prompt: Which of these problems are about a WHOLE GROUP of values (pick all that apply)?
options: The prices of every item in a cart
exercises.explanation: A cart of prices and hourly temperatures are both groups of many values. A single house number or one score is just one value.

exercises.prompt: What is a 'collection' (also called a list)?
options: One thing that holds many values in order
exercises.explanation: A collection is a single container holding many values, kept in order. That's the big new idea of this lap.

exercises.prompt: Match each real-world group to the kind of values it holds.
exercises.explanation: Groups hold many values; a lone fact holds one. Spotting which you have tells you whether you need a list.

exercises.prompt: A collection lets you keep many values together under one name, instead of inventing a separate variable for each.
exercises.explanation: Imagine 100 scores. You don't want 100 variables. One list holds all of them — that's why collections exist.

exercises.prompt: You have the ages of 30 students. Without a collection, what would you be forced to do?
options: Make 30 separate variables, one per student
Use just one variable for all 30
Nothing — one number can hold 30 values
exercises.explanation: Thirty separate variables would be painful. A collection holds all 30 together, which is far simpler.

exercises.prompt: Which word signals a problem is probably about a collection?
exercises.explanation: Words like each, all, and every point at a whole group. They're a strong hint you'll want a list.

exercises.prompt: This unit is MEET — just the idea. What will you learn to actually write next?
options: How to create a list of values
How to count to a million
exercises.explanation: Now that you can recognize a 'many values' problem, the next lessons show how to write a list down in code.
